subject: anatomy
title: Fascia and triangles of the neck

steps.tx: The **deep cervical fascia** has three layers: the **investing layer**, the **pretracheal layer** and the **prevertebral layer**. The investing layer surrounds the neck and splits to enclose the parotid and submandibular glands. The pretracheal layer wraps the thyroid, trachea and oesophagus. The prevertebral layer lies in front of the vertebral column and gives an extension around the brachial plexus and subclavian artery, forming the axillary sheath.

The investing layer surrounds the neck and splits to enclose the parotid and submandibular glands. The pretracheal layer wraps the thyroid, trachea and oesophagus. steps.tx: The **carotid sheath** is a fascial tube holding the **common carotid artery**, the **internal jugular vein** and the **vagus nerve**. The internal and external carotid arteries are branches of the common carotid, so the sheath encloses the common and internal carotid arteries but not the external carotid. The **retropharyngeal space** lies behind the pharynx, extending from the base of skull down to the posterior mediastinum through the retrovisceral space.
steps.say: The carotid sheath is a fascial tube holding the common carotid artery, the internal jugular vein and the vagus nerve. It encloses the common and internal carotid arteries but not the external carotid. The retropharyngeal space lies behind the pharynx, extending from the base of skull down into the posterior mediastinum through the retrovisceral space.

steps.tx: The **danger area** of the neck lies between the **alar fascia** and the prevertebral fascia proper. Pus here can spread into the posterior mediastinum. **Ludwig angina** is a rapidly spreading cellulitis of the submandibular spaces, usually from dental infection, that can compromise the airway. Treat it as an emergency with airway protection and antibiotics.

steps.tx: **Sternocleidomastoid** is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve. When one muscle contracts it turns the chin to the opposite side and tilts the head to the same side. Damage to the muscle or its nerve causes weakness in turning the head against resistance, and the classic lesion-testing manoeuvre is to ask the patient to turn the head against the examiner's hand. In **torticollis**, the muscle is shortened, producing a tilted head and rotated chin.
